messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 71
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Lawyer
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 71

Mrs. Tran is a 71-year-old retired attorney who spent forty-three years practicing family law. She still attends bar association meetings and occasionally consults for younger colleagues. She is small-framed, with silver hair pulled back in a neat bun, and she sits very upright in the chair, hands folded in her lap, as though she is about to deliver closing arguments. But her voice, when she describes the assault, is barely above a whisper.

It happened eighteen months ago, after a late-night hearing at the downtown courthouse. She had won a difficult custody case and felt the familiar, quiet satisfaction of a well-argued motion. The parking garage was nearly empty. She remembers the hum of the fluorescent lights, the smell of damp concrete. A man came up behind her as she reached her car. He demanded her purse. She handed it over without a word. Then he pushed her hard against the driver’s side door, grabbed her wrist, and pulled off her wedding ring. She did not scream. She had learned, over a lifetime, that screaming did not always help. When he was gone, she drove home with shaking hands, told her husband she had been robbed, and went to bed.

For the first month, she told herself it was just a purse snatching. She was not injured. The ring was insured. She filed a police report, gave a brief statement, and went back to work. But soon she found herself taking the stairs instead of the elevator in the garage. Then she started parking three blocks away, in a surface lot with no walls. Then she stopped attending late hearings entirely, delegating them to associates without explanation. She told herself it was age—she was nearly seventy, it made sense to slow down—but she knew, deep down, that it was not age. It was the garage. It was the dark. It was the sound of footsteps behind her.

Now she no longer goes downtown at all. She meets colleagues for coffee only at midday, in cafes with wide windows and clear sightlines. She has stopped walking her dog after sunset. Her husband, a retired pharmacist, tries to hold her hand when they take their evening stroll, but she flinches—not from him, but from the sensation of being touched from behind without warning. She has not told him about the flinching. She has not told anyone about the dreams.

At night she dreams of the concrete floor of the garage. In the dream, she is running, but her legs are slow, and the fluorescent lights flicker. She wakes with her heart pounding, her palms pressed flat against the mattress, as though bracing for a fall. She does not wake her husband. She lies still and counts the seconds until dawn.

Her memory has become unreliable. She forgets appointments, misplaces her reading glasses, struggles to follow the threads of legal arguments she once mastered effortlessly. At a recent bar association luncheon, a colleague asked her opinion on a child custody statute. She opened her mouth and found nothing—just the hum of the garage lights. She excused herself and went home.

She is not afraid of being alone. She is afraid of the moment just before being alone, when someone is still there, behind her, and she cannot see them. She checks the back seat of her car every time she drives. She locks the doors three times. She avoids mirrors in dim lighting, because sometimes the reflection of her own shoulder startles her.

She knows she is a lawyer. She knows the facts of the case. She knows the assault was brief, non-sexual, and that she was not physically harmed. But knowing does not change the way her chest tightens when the elevator doors close. It does not change the way she stands in her own kitchen, frozen, because her husband called her name from the hallway and she did not hear him approach.

She is here now, in this office, because her daughter begged her. She sits very upright. She tells the story without tears. And when she finishes, she looks at the clock and says, “I don’t know why I can’t let it go. I’ve won harder cases than this.”
